text: Amrita Sher-Gil (30 January 1913 – 5 December 1941) was a Hungarian–Indian painter recognized as "one of the greatest avant-garde women artists of the early 20th century" and a pioneer in modern Indian art. She began painting from an early age, receiving formal art lessons at eight and painting servants in her household as a child, an experience that later influenced her return to India. Born Dalma-Amrita on 30 January 1913 at 4 Szilágyi Dezső square, Budapest, then part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, she was the daughter of Umrao Singh Sher-Gil Majithia, a Punjabi Indian Jat Sikh aristocrat and scholar in Sanskrit and Persian, and Marie Antoinette Gottesman, a Hungarian-Jewish opera singer from an affluent bourgeois family. Her parents first met in 1912 in Lahore, and her mother came to India as a companion to Princess Bamba Sutherland, granddaughter of Maharaja Ranjit Singh. Sher-Gil was the elder of two daughters; her younger sister was Indira Sundaram (née Sher-Gil, born March 1914), mother of artist Vivan Sundaram. The family remained in Budapest until after the First World War. She was the niece of Indologist Ervin Baktay, who noticed her artistic talent during a 1926 visit to Shimla and advocated for her to pursue art, guiding her through critiques and academic training. In 1921, the family moved to Summer Hill, Shimla, India, where Sher-Gil began studying piano and violin and, by age nine, performed in concerts and plays at the Gaiety Theatre. She was expelled from her Catholic school, Convent of Jesus and Mary, for declaring herself an atheist. In 1924, after meeting an Italian sculptor in Shimla, her mother moved to Florence, where Sher-Gil enrolled at Santa Annunziata, exposing her to Italian masters, though she returned to India shortly after. At sixteen, she traveled to Europe with her mother to train in Paris, first at the Académie de la Grande Chaumière under Pierre Vaillent and Lucien Simon (where she met Boris Taslitzky) and later at the École des Beaux-Arts (1930–1934). She drew inspiration from Paul Cézanne, Paul Gauguin, and Amedeo Modigliani, and her work in Paris showed a maturity rarely seen in a 16-year-old. In 1931, she was briefly engaged to Yusuf Ali Khan, with rumors of an affair with her first cousin and later husband Viktor Egan; her letters reveal same-sex affairs. Her early works displayed Post-Impressionist influences, and her 1932 oil painting *Young Girls* marked a breakthrough, earning her a gold medal and election as an Associate of the Grand Salon in Paris in 1933—making her the youngest ever member and the only Asian to receive this honor. Her Paris period included self-portraits, nude studies, still lifes, and portraits of friends. One of her professors noted that her rich color palette suggested she was not at home in Europe, and that her true artistic atmosphere lay in the East. In 1933, she began feeling a strong longing to return to India, which she did at the end of 1934. In May 1935, she met English journalist Malcolm Muggeridge, with whom she had a brief intense affair and painted a portrait now held by the National Gallery of Modern Art in New Delhi. By September 1935, she saw him off for England. In 1936, at the behest of art collector and critic Karl Khandalavala, she traveled to India to explore her Indian roots, where she was deeply influenced by Mughal and Pahari schools of painting and the Ajanta cave paintings. In 1937, she toured South India and produced her South Indian trilogy—*Bride's Toilet*, *Brahmacharis*, and *South Indian Villagers Going to Market*—reflecting her passion for color and empathy for impoverished subjects. She declared, "I can only paint in India. Europe belongs to Picasso, Matisse, Braque.... India belongs only to me," marking a shift in her artistic mission to depict Indian life. Her work during this phase, including *Village Scene*, *In the Ladies' Enclosure*, and *Siesta*, showed influences from miniature and Pahari schools. Though acclaimed by critics like Karl Khandalavala and Charles Fabri as the greatest painter of the century, her paintings found few buyers; the Nawab Salar Jung of Hyderabad returned them, and the Maharaja of Mysore chose Raja Ravi Varma's works. A Congress sympathizer, Sher-Gil was drawn to the poor and distressed, and her depictions of Indian villagers and women reflect their conditions. She admired Gandhi’s philosophy and lifestyle, and Nehru was charmed by her beauty and talent; he visited her at Saraya in October 1940 and attended her 1937 exhibition in New Delhi. Though she exchanged letters with Nehru, her parents burned them when she was away marrying in Budapest. In September 1941, Sher-Gil and Viktor Egan moved to Lahore, where she lived and painted at 23 Ganga Ram Mansions, The Mall. She was known for her affairs with both men and women, and painted several of her female lovers; *Two Women* is believed to depict her and her lover Marie Louise. Her later works include *Tahitian* (1937), *Red Brick House* (1938), *Hill Scene* (1938), and *The Bride* (1940); her last work was left unfinished just before her death. In 1941, at age 28, she became seriously ill just days before her first major solo show in Lahore, slipping into a coma and dying around midnight on 5 December 1941. The cause of death remains unknown; a failed abortion and subsequent peritonitis have been suggested, and her mother accused her husband Egan of murdering her. The day after her death, Britain declared war on Hungary, and Egan was interned as an enemy alien. Sher-Gil was cremated on 7 December 1941 in Lahore. Her art has influenced generations of Indian artists, including Sayed Haider Raza and Arpita Singh, and her depictions of women have made her a beacon for women globally. The Government of India has declared her works National Art Treasures, with most housed in the National Gallery of Modern Art in New Delhi and some at the Lahore Museum. A postage stamp featuring her painting *Hill Women* was released in 1978 by India Post, and Amrita Shergil Marg is a road in Lutyens' Delhi named after her. Her work proved to Western societies that Indians could create fine art, and when sold in India, the government mandates that the art remain in the country—fewer than ten of her works have been sold globally. In 2006, *Village Scene* sold for ₹6.9 crores at an auction in New Delhi, the highest price ever paid for an Indian painting at the time. The Indian cultural centre in Budapest is named the Amrita Sher-Gil Cultural Centre. Contemporary artists have recreated her works. The 1969 documentary *Amrita Sher-Gil*, directed by Bhagwan Das Garga and produced by India’s Films Division, won the National Film Award for Best Non-Feature Film. In 1993, she inspired the Urdu play *Tumhari Amrita*. UNESCO designated 2013, the 100th anniversary of her birth, as the International Year of Amrita Sher-Gil. Her work is a key theme in the novel *Faking It* by Amrita Chowdhury. Aurora Zogoiby, a character in Salman Rushdie’s *The Moor’s Last Sigh* (1995), was inspired by Sher-Gil. Claire Kohda references Sher-Gil and her painting *The Three Girls* in her 2022 novel *Woman, Eating*, where the protagonist, Lydia, identifies with the subjects and speculates they were vampires. Sher-Gil was sometimes called India’s Frida Kahlo due to her revolutionary blending of Western and traditional art forms. On 30 January 2016, Google celebrated her 103rd birthday with a Doodle. In 2018, *The New York Times* published a belated obituary. That year, at a Sotheby’s auction in Mumbai, *The Little Girl in Blue* (a 1934 portrait of her cousin Babit, aged eight) sold for a record-breaking 18.69 crores. In 2021, *Portrait of Denyse* (1932, featuring Parisian art critic Denyse Proutaux) was auctioned by Christie’s with an estimated value of $1.8–2.8 million; Proutaux appeared in other Sher-Gil paintings, including *Young Girls* and *Denise Proutaux*, both exhibited in the "Amrita Shergil: The Passionate Quest" show at the National Gallery of Modern Art in New Delhi. On 18 September 2023, her 1937 painting *The Story Teller* fetched $7.4 million (Rs 61.8 crore) at a SaffronArt auction, setting a record for the highest price achieved by an Indian artist—just 10 days after Syed Haider Raza’s *Gestation* sold for ₹51.7 crore at Pundole.
